title: Sadhguru on Amavasya: Why Tonight's New Moon Is Spiritually Significant
excerpt: September's Amavasya tithi runs tonight into tomorrow morning. Sadhguru explains why the moon's absence makes its presence more powerful — and why the new moon suits the hardworking and tough.
body:
• September's Amavasya — the new moon — falls tonight into tomorrow morning: the Amavasya tithi runs from 10:33 am on September 10 to 8:56 am on September 11, in the month of Virgo (Bhadrapada).
  • Sadhguru's framing: "Whenever something or somebody becomes absent, through that absence, their presence always becomes more powerful" — on Amavasya, the moon's absence makes her presence felt even more.
  • "The earth broods on Amavasya; the life process is slowed down on the planet... integration of life happens much better on this day," he says, making it a day for spiritual sadhana and self-awareness: "What is me and what is not me."
  • His distinction: "Pournami is love, and Amavasya is aggression" — Amavasya suits the hardworking and tough, while the full moon suits the sensitive and subtle.

Tonight the moon disappears — and for Sadhguru, that absence is the whole point. September's Amavasya, the new moon tithi running from 10:33 am today to 8:56 am tomorrow morning, is what the Isha founder calls one of the most potent nights of the month for inner work.

The power of absence

"Amavasya means no moon day or new moon day. Whenever something or somebody becomes absent, through that absence, their presence always becomes more powerful," Sadhguru says. "You do not really feel their presence when they are around. Only when they are gone, the vacuum that they have left behind has become more powerful than their presence itself."

Applied to the moon, the logic is poetic: on Amavasya, he says, "her absence makes her more present than ever before... on Amavasya, the presence is felt even more."

A day the earth broods

Sadhguru describes Amavasya as a day of natural slowdown. "The earth broods on Amavasya; the life process is slowed down on the planet... integration of life happens much better on this day." That slowing, he says, lets a practitioner notice the body as something separate from the self: "Very clearly a distance arises" — making it a day for spiritual sadhana.

"Amavasya is a day when one can become easily aware of, 'What is me and what is not me,' and from there on, the journey from untruth to truth begins."

— Sadhguru

Aggression versus love

He draws a sharp line between the two poles of the lunar month: "Pournami is love, and Amavasya is aggression... for a hardworking, tough, aggressive person, Amavasya is definitely an important aspect. For a person who is very sensitive and subtle, Pournami is a very important aspect."

The practice angle is elemental: on Amavasya nights, traditional guidance includes simple grounding practices — walking barefoot, connecting with the earth. At the Isha Yoga Center, the Dhyanalinga receives ksheera (milk) offerings from 6 am to 12:30 pm and jala (water) from 12:30 pm to 8 pm on Amavasya and Purnima days.

Background: why Amavasya matters in the Hindu calendar

Amavasya nights carry special weight in the Hindu calendar — the most significant being Mahalaya Amavasya, the beginning of the Dussehra season, when ancestor offerings (Pitru Paksha tarpan) are made. This September's new moon falls in Bhadrapada, the month leading into the festive season. Whether approached as ritual, rest or reflection, Sadhguru's core invitation stays simple: use the moonless night to notice what usually goes unnoticed.
